screens.title: Managing Identities and Wallets
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we learn how client applications obtain, store, and use the cryptographic identities required to interact with a Hyperledger Fabric network. You will understand what an identity is — a public X.509 certificate paired with a private key — and why Fabric requires authenticated identities for every transaction. We'll show the practical wallet options provided by the Node. js SDK, how to enroll an administrator and an application user, and the two-step registration-and-enrollment flow with the Fabric Certificate Authority. You will also see concrete scripts used during development, and a short discussion of the security tradeoffs of storing private keys on disk versus using dedicated key management. By the end you should be able to enroll an admin, register and enroll an app user, import credentials into a filesystem wallet, and connect an application to the Gateway using an application identity. Consider how the principle of least privilege shapes which identity you choose for day-to-day operations. Ready to explore the code and the security decisions that follow?

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Every Fabric client action must be signed by an X.509 identity; wallets centralize secure storage of those certificates and private keys.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Managing Identities
Managing Identities and Wallets
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

This chapter shows how identities are represented, how wallets store them, and the standard registration and enrollment flow using the Fabric CA. Examples use the Node.js SDK and filesystem wallets for development.

Why this matters

Fabric is permissioned: every request must be authenticated and authorized. Proper identity handling prevents impersonation, enforces least privilege, and enables auditable transactions.

Who this affects

Application developers, DevOps teams deploying clients, and security engineers who must protect private keys and integrate with enterprise key stores.

Explore Key Topics
Identity Composition
X.509 certificate + private key define an identity used to sign transactions.
Wallet Types
File system wallets persist identities; in-memory wallets are ephemeral for tests.
Register & Enroll
Admins register users with the CA; users enroll to get a certificate and key.
Concept Map
Identity
X.509 certificate and private key used to sign transactions.
Wallet
Abstract storage for identities: persistent or ephemeral.
Registration & Enrollment
Two-step CA interaction to obtain credentials and add them to a wallet.
Getting started

You'll run two scripts during the lab: one to enroll an admin and another to register and enroll an application user. The wallet directory will show stored identities after each step.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: We will focus on four practical competencies that you can apply immediately. First, you will explain how identities and wallets enable secure, authenticated interactions with a Fabric network. That includes naming the parts of an X.509 identity and why both certificate and private key are required. Second, you'll distinguish admin and application user identities, understanding who should perform enrollment, registration, and day-to-day operations. Third, you will implement and operate a file system–based wallet using the Node. js SDK: create it, check for identities, and import credentials. Fourth, you will register and enroll a new application user with a CA and import the resulting certificate and key into the wallet. Each skill includes a simple verification step so you can confirm competency, like checking the wallet directory for a new identity file. These objectives prepare you to manage identities responsibly and avoid common pitfalls when building Fabric client applications.

screens.title: Objectives: Security and Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: Beyond workflows, this chapter teaches practical security decisions. You will learn the risks of storing private keys on local filesystems, and why production systems often use HSMs or cloud key management. We'll explain how the SDK integrates with external key stores, and what measures you should check—file permissions, access control, and secret management—before trusting a wallet on disk. You will also practice spotting two frequent mistakes: trying to enroll a user before an admin is enrolled, and registering with an incorrect affiliation in multi-organization setups. Each objective includes a short verification step so you can validate your environment. By mastering these practices you reduce the chance of impersonation and make deployments safer for real-world business channels. Objectives: Security and Best Practices means private keys require stronger protection than files; plan for hsms, cloud kms, or strict file permissions in production.. In practical terms, protecting private keys and avoiding common mistakes. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Security Objectives
Security Best Practices

Understand the threat model: the private key can be used to impersonate an identity. In production, move keys to hardware or cloud-managed services. Use the SDK interfaces that support external key stores rather than persisting raw private key files.

Checks
  • Confirm wallet permissions prevent broad access.
  • Use least-privilege identities for app connections.
  • Plan for key rotation and revocation processes.
When to use HSM/KMS

If private keys must be protected from filesystem compromise or audited by enterprise policy, integrate with an HSM or cloud key store supported by the Fabric SDK.

Common Mistakes

Enroll users only after an admin exists. Check affiliation values during registration to avoid CA rejections in multi-org setups.

Key Takeaway

Treat private keys as high-value secrets: if in doubt, use a managed key service rather than persistent files for production deployments.

screens.title: What is an Identity in Fabric?
screens.narratorSegment: An identity in Hyperledger Fabric is the cryptographic bundle that proves a requester's identity and authority. Practically, it consists of an X.509 certificate and its matching private key. The certificate contains the public key and identifying attributes issued by the organization’s Certificate Authority; the private key is kept secret and is used to digitally sign transactions. Signing is what binds intent to actions on the ledger and enables authorization checks. A concrete example is an identity labeled Admin@org1. example. com: the certificate lists the subject and any attributes, and the private key proves the admin signed the enrollment or registration calls. A common misconception is that the certificate alone is sufficient; without the private key you cannot sign transactions, so the certificate is not enough to perform authenticated calls. In practice you must protect both parts, and your client code must present them to the Gateway or SDK in a way that keeps the key confidential. To check you understand, inspect the wallet after enrollment and confirm both certificate and private key are stored together. Why does Fabric require this pairing? Because signatures provide non-repudiation and authorization, and the private key is the authority gate.

keyIdea.title: Identity definition
keyIdea.text: An identity is the certificate plus the private key; both are required for authenticated transactions and authorization.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Identity
Definition

An identity is a set of cryptographic credentials: an X.509 certificate and a private key. The certificate identifies the subject and is issued by the CA; the private key is used for signing requests.

Analogy
Think of the certificate as an ID card and the private key as your signature stamp. The card alone proves who you are, but only the stamp proves you approved an action.
Key Takeaway

Both pieces are required: without a private key the certificate cannot sign transactions, and without the certificate the network cannot validate the public key’s identity.

Identity Structure
Certificate (X.509)
Contains the public key, subject name, issuer, and attributes assigned by the CA.
Private Key
Kept secret by the owner; used to sign transactions so the network can verify authorship.
Example: Admin@org1.example.com
Certificate: -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE----- ... -----END CERTIFICATE----- Private Key: -----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY----- ... -----END PRIVATE KEY-----
Common misconception
Believing the certificate alone grants access. Without the private key you cannot prove authority to act.
Check your understanding
After enrollment, inspect the wallet to confirm both certificate and private key are present for the identity name used.

screens.title: Wallet Types in the Node.js SDK
screens.narratorSegment: The Fabric Node. js SDK exposes wallet implementations to manage identities. The two most common are the persistent file system wallet and the ephemeral in-memory wallet. A file system wallet persists credentials to disk so that identities survive application restarts and are available to the Gateway across sessions. This is typically used for long-running client applications and development environments where you want predictable persistence. By contrast, an in-memory wallet keeps identities only in process memory. It is useful for tests, short-lived scripts, or when persistence is not desired for security reasons. A practical example: during development you might use Wallets. newFileSystemWallet to store admin and appUser credentials in a wallet folder. For automated unit tests you might prefer Wallets. newInMemoryWallet so tests start clean each run. A common pitfall is assuming a file system wallet is secure by default; file permissions and storage location matter. For production, plan for external key management; the SDK lets you integrate with hardware or cloud stores. To validate your knowledge, create a wallet, add an identity, restart the application, and confirm the identity persists only with the file system wallet.

keyIdea.title: Wallet choice
keyIdea.text: Use a file system wallet for persistence and an in-memory wallet for ephemeral scenarios; evaluate security accordingly.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Wallet Types
File System Wallet

Creates a wallet directory on disk that stores identity entries persistently. Use Wallets.newFileSystemWallet(path) to create or open this wallet.

When to use
  • Long-running applications that must persist credentials.
  • Development environments where convenience matters.
Example: Wallets.newFileSystemWallet('./wallet')
In-Memory Wallet

Stores identities only in process memory and is cleared when the process exits. Useful for tests and scenarios where no persistence is desired.

When to use
  • Unit tests and ephemeral scripts.
  • Scenarios that require no disk artifacts.
Example: Wallets.newInMemoryWallet()
Security note
Persistence requires secure file permissions; consider HSM or cloud KMS for production-grade key protection.
Developer tip
Use file system wallets for manual labs and switch to managed key stores for deployments subject to compliance requirements.
Check
Add identity, restart app, and verify identity remains with file system wallet but not with in-memory wallet.

screens.title: Registration and Enrollment
screens.narratorSegment: Fabric uses a two-step process with the Certificate Authority to add new application users: registration followed by enrollment. Registration is performed by an existing administrator identity and tells the CA about the new user, setting attributes such as enrollment ID, role, and affiliation. The CA returns an enrollment secret after successful registration. Enrollment is the second step where the user or the client acting on behalf of the user sends that secret back to the CA and requests the certificate and key pair. The CA verifies the secret and issues the X.509 certificate and private key material. A concrete scenario is registering appUser under org1. department1; the admin registers with the affiliation and the CA then returns a secret. The client uses that secret in an enroll call to obtain credentials. A typical mistake is trying to enroll without a valid enrollment secret or before the admin is enrolled; both lead to failures. To validate this flow, follow the enrollAdmin and registerUser scripts in the lab: you will see the admin identity imported first, and then the app user after registration and enrollment complete.

keyIdea.title: Registration → Enrollment
keyIdea.text: Registration records the user and returns a secret. Enrollment exchanges that secret for the certificate and private key.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Registration & Enrollment
Process: Register then Enroll
Step 1 — Registration
An admin calls the CA to register a new user, specifying enrollmentID, role, and affiliation. The CA returns an enrollment secret to the requester.
Step 2 — Enrollment
The user uses the enrollment secret to request their certificate and private key from the CA. On success, the credentials are returned for storage in a wallet.
Example
Admin registers appUser with affiliation org1.department1, receives a secret, and then appUser enrolls using that secret to get credentials.
Misconception
Assuming registration issues credentials directly. Registration only creates the record and returns a secret; enrollment issues the certificate and key.
Check
After registration and enrollment, confirm the wallet contains the new identity and that the certificate and private key exist for that name.

screens.title: Create and Inspect a File System Wallet
screens.narratorSegment: This lesson walks through the common code pattern to create a persistent wallet, check for an existing identity, and print the wallet path. The Node. js SDK supplies Wallets. newFileSystemWallet which returns a wallet object with methods such as get and put. In practice you define the walletPath in your project, create the wallet at that location, and then query for an identity name such as admin or appUser. A concrete example appears in the enrollAdmin script: the code constructs walletPath from the current working directory and calls await Wallets. newFileSystemWallet(walletPath). After that a call to wallet. get('admin') returns either the stored identity or undefined. A common mistake is failing to await wallet operations or assuming get will throw when the identity is missing; instead it returns undefined. In the lab you will create a wallet, verify the printed wallet path, and confirm identities appear in the directory. This pattern is the foundation for adding or retrieving identities before connecting the Gateway. Create and Inspect a File System Wallet means use wallets.newfilesystemwallet to persist identities and wallet.get to check presence before enrollment or gateway connections.. In practical terms, using wallets.newfilesystemwallet and wallet.get. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Wallet pattern
keyIdea.text: Use Wallets.newFileSystemWallet to persist identities and wallet.get to check presence before enrollment or Gateway connections.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › File System Wallet
Pattern
  1. Create wallet path in your project.
  2. Call Wallets.newFileSystemWallet(path) and await the result.
  3. Check for identity with wallet.get(name).
  4. Put identity with wallet.put(name, x509Identity) after enrollment.
Common mistake

Not awaiting wallet creation or assuming wallet.get throws on missing identity. Handle get returning undefined.

Code sample
'use strict';

const { Wallets } = require('hyperledger-fabric-network');
const path = require('path');

async function example() {
  const walletPath = path.join(process.cwd(), 'wallet');
  const wallet = await Wallets.newFileSystemWallet(walletPath);
  console.log(`Wallet path: ${walletPath}`);

  const identity = await wallet.get('admin');
  if (identity) {
    console.log('Admin identity exists in the wallet');
  } else {
    console.log('No admin identity found');
  }
}

example();
Example outcome
After running this code you should see the printed wallet directory and a message indicating whether the admin identity exists.
Check
Use the wallet directory listing to confirm that identity files were created after enrollment.

screens.title: enrollAdmin.js — Enroll the Admin Identity
screens.narratorSegment: The enrollAdmin. js script is a typical development helper that enrolls an organization admin with the CA and stores the returned credentials in a filesystem wallet. It loads the network configuration, creates a Fabric CA client object, and constructs a wallet path. The script checks whether the admin identity already exists in the wallet; if it does, it exits to avoid overwriting existing credentials. If not present, it calls ca. enroll with the enrollment ID and secret—commonly admin and adminpw in test networks—and builds an X.509 identity object containing the certificate, private key, and the organization's MSP identifier. The identity is then stored with wallet. put. An important practical note: in production the enrollment secret will differ and admin identities may be provisioned differently. A common pitfall is not loading the correct CA information from the connection profile, which leads to failed enroll calls. After running this script you should see a wallet directory containing the admin identity and be prepared to register additional users. enrollAdmin.js — Enroll the Admin Identity means enrolls admin via ca and stores certificate and private key in the wallet for subsequent registration tasks.. In practical terms, walkthrough of the admin enrollment script. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Enroll admin script
keyIdea.text: Enrolls admin via CA and stores certificate and private key in the wallet for subsequent registration tasks.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › enrollAdmin.js
Script excerpt
'use strict';

const { Wallets } = require('hyperledger-fabric-network');
const FabricCAServices = require('fabric-ca-client');
const path = require('path');
const fs = require('fs');

async function main() {
  try {
    const ccpPath = path.resolve(__dirname, 'connection-org1.json');
    const ccp = JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync(ccpPath, 'utf8'));

    const caInfo = ccp.certificateAuthorities['ca.org1.example.com'];
    const caTLSCACerts = caInfo.tlsCACerts.path;
    const ca = new FabricCAServices(caInfo.url, { trustedRoots: caTLSCACerts, verify: false }, caInfo.caName);

    const walletPath = path.join(process.cwd(), 'wallet');
    const wallet = await Wallets.newFileSystemWallet(walletPath);

    const identity = await wallet.get('admin');
    if (identity) {
      console.log('An identity for the admin user "admin" already exists in the wallet');
      return;
    }

    const enrollment = await ca.enroll({ enrollmentID: 'admin', enrollmentSecret: 'adminpw' });
    const x509Identity = {
      credentials: {
        certificate: enrollment.certificate,
        privateKey: enrollment.key.toBytes(),
      },
      mspId: 'Org1MSP',
      type: 'X.509',
    };
    await wallet.put('admin', x509Identity);
    console.log('Successfully enrolled admin user "admin" and imported it into the wallet');

  } catch (error) {
    console.error(`Failed to enroll admin user "admin": ${error}`);
    process.exit(1);
  }
}

main();
What to watch
Confirm the connection profile points to the correct CA url and caName. If CA info is wrong, enrollment fails.
After running
Inspect the wallet directory for the admin identity and ensure file permissions are restrictive in sensitive environments.

screens.title: registerUser.js — Register and Enroll appUser
screens.narratorSegment: The registerUser. js script demonstrates the complete registration and enrollment flow for an application user. It first loads the network configuration and CA information, creates or opens a file system wallet, and checks whether appUser is already present. If appUser is missing, the script checks that the admin identity exists in the wallet—without it registration cannot proceed. The script obtains a UserContext from the wallet provider for the admin identity, then calls ca. register to register appUser with affiliation and role. The CA returns an enrollment secret, which the script uses in ca. enroll to obtain certificate and private key materials. Finally, it constructs an X.509 identity object and stores it with wallet. put. Pay attention to the affiliation argument: in multi-organization setups it must match an affiliation configured in the CA, otherwise registration will fail. After this script completes, your wallet should contain both admin and appUser identities and your application can connect using the appUser identity for normal operations. registerUser.js — Register and Enroll appUser means register uses the admin to request an enrollment secret; enroll exchanges that secret for credentials which are imported into the wallet.. In practical terms, how the script registers and imports appuser into the wallet. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Register & enroll script
keyIdea.text: Register uses the admin to request an enrollment secret; enroll exchanges that secret for credentials which are imported into the wallet.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › registerUser.js
Script excerpt
'use strict';

const { Gateway, Wallets } = require('hyperledger-fabric-network');
const FabricCAServices = require('fabric-ca-client');
const path = require('path');
const fs = require('fs');

async function main() {
  try {
    const ccpPath = path.resolve(__dirname, 'connection-org1.json');
    const ccp = JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync(ccpPath, 'utf8'));

    const caInfo = ccp.certificateAuthorities['ca.org1.example.com'];
    const caTLSCACerts = caInfo.tlsCACerts.path;
    const ca = new FabricCAServices(caInfo.url, { trustedRoots: caTLSCACerts, verify: false }, caInfo.caName);

    const walletPath = path.join(process.cwd(), 'wallet');
    const wallet = await Wallets.newFileSystemWallet(walletPath);

    const userIdentity = await wallet.get('appUser');
    if (userIdentity) {
      console.log('An identity for the user "appUser" already exists in the wallet');
      return;
    }

    const adminIdentity = await wallet.get('admin');
    if (!adminIdentity) {
      console.log('An identity for the admin user "admin" does not exist in the wallet');
      console.log('Run the enrollAdmin.js application before retrying');
      return;
    }

    const provider = wallet.getProviderRegistry().getProvider(adminIdentity.type);
    const adminUser = await provider.getUserContext(adminIdentity, 'admin');

    const secret = await ca.register({
      affiliation: 'org1.department1',
      enrollmentID: 'appUser',
      role: 'client'
    }, adminUser);

    const enrollment = await ca.enroll({
      enrollmentID: 'appUser',
      enrollmentSecret: secret
    });

    const x509Identity = {
      credentials: {
        certificate: enrollment.certificate,
        privateKey: enrollment.key.toBytes(),
      },
      mspId: 'Org1MSP',
      type: 'X.509',
    };
    await wallet.put('appUser', x509Identity);
    console.log('Successfully registered and enrolled user "appUser" and imported it into the wallet');

  } catch (error) {
    console.error(`Failed to register user "appUser": ${error}`);
    process.exit(1);
  }
}

main();
Affiliation gotcha
Ensure the affiliation matches the CA configuration; incorrect values cause registration failures in multi-org setups.
Post-check
Verify wallet now contains both admin and appUser entries before attempting Gateway connections.

screens.title: Protecting Private Keys
screens.narratorSegment: Private keys are the single most sensitive element of a Fabric identity: possession of a private key allows an actor to sign transactions as the identity owner, which can enable impersonation and fraudulent ledger actions. For development, filesystem wallets are convenient, but in production you must consider hardened key storage. The chapter recommends Hardware Security Modules (HSMs) or cloud-managed key services like Azure Key Vault as options to remove raw key material from application files. The Fabric SDK exposes interfaces to integrate with such key stores rather than persisting private keys directly in files. Practical mitigations include strict file permissions on wallet directories, limited administrative access to the host, encrypted disks, and auditing of key usage. A common misconception is that encrypting the wallet file is sufficient without access controls; encryption helps, but key lifecycle management, rotation, and revocation policies are equally important. A concrete step is to evaluate whether your deployment requires a managed key service and, if so, plan integration with the Fabric client to delegate signing to that service. Ask yourself: if a private key were lost, how quickly could you revoke it and issue a replacement?

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Private Key Security
Why private keys matter

Possession of a private key allows anyone to sign transactions as that identity. In business networks this can lead to fraudulent ledger entries and a breakdown of trust.

Mitigations
  • Use HSMs or cloud KMS for production.
  • Restrict filesystem permissions and audit access.
  • Plan key rotation and revocation procedures.
SDK integration
The Fabric SDK supports interfaces that enable delegating signing operations to external key stores instead of exporting raw private keys to files.
Common misconception

Assuming file encryption alone is enough. Access control, key lifecycle, and separation of duties are also necessary for robust security.

Quick check
If an identity key is leaked, can you revoke it and re-enroll users quickly? If not, your key management needs improvement.

screens.title: Admin vs Application User Identities
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding identity roles is crucial for correct and secure operations. An admin identity is given elevated privileges within an organization’s CA: it can register new users and define their attributes. Admins are typically used only for onboarding identities and should not be used for normal application traffic. Application user identities, such as appUser, are regular user credentials enrolled by the CA and granted the minimal set of permissions required to interact with chaincode. This separation adheres to least privilege: administrative tasks are separated from everyday transactions so an attacker gaining an app user's key cannot perform admin-level actions. A practical example is enrolling an admin to register and enroll an appUser, then configuring your application to use appUser for all Gateway connections. A common mistake is embedding admin credentials into production apps for convenience; this significantly increases risk because those credentials can register or revoke identities. To validate, ensure your app connects using appUser and that wallet contains both admin—used only for registration—and appUser used by the runtime. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Debugging Tips
screens.narratorSegment: When working with the CA and wallets you will encounter a few recurrent issues. First, enrollment failures often stem from incorrect CA information in the connection profile—URL, caName, or TLS settings must match the CA configuration. screens.title: Where Wallets Fit in an Application
screens.narratorSegment: Wallets sit between your client application and two external systems: the Fabric Certificate Authority and the network Gateway. The CA issues credentials during enrollment; the wallet stores those credentials. When your application connects, the Gateway uses the identity retrieved from the wallet to authenticate and sign requests to peers and orderers. Conceptually, the flow is: enroll admin with CA → admin registers a user → user enrolls and credentials are stored in wallet → application retrieves identity from wallet and connects to Gateway. In development, the wallet is often a local filesystem directory; in production, the wallet may be an adapter to an HSM or cloud KMS so private keys never leave the secure store. The architecture highlights the importance of consistent wallet paths, secure storage, and role separation: admin artifacts are only needed for identity lifecycle management, while runtime only needs application identities. To verify architecture correctness, follow the lab steps and confirm each interaction succeeds and that the wallet exposes expected identities to your runtime environment. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we learn how client applications obtain, store, and use the cryptographic identities required to interact with a Hyperledger Fabric network. You will understand what an identity is — a public X.509 certificate paired with a private key — and why Fabric requires authenticated identities for every transaction. We'll show the practical wallet options provided by the Node. js SDK, how to enroll an administrator and an application user, and the two-step registration-and-enrollment flow with the Fabric Certificate Authority. You will also see concrete scripts used during development, and a short discussion of the security tradeoffs of storing private keys on disk versus using dedicated key management. By the end you should be able to enroll an admin, register and enroll an app user, import credentials into a filesystem wallet, and connect an application to the Gateway using an application identity. Consider how the principle of least privilege shapes which identity you choose for day-to-day operations. Ready to explore the code and the security decisions that follow?

We will focus on four practical competencies that you can apply immediately. First, you will explain how identities and wallets enable secure, authenticated interactions with a Fabric network. That includes naming the parts of an X.509 identity and why both certificate and private key are required. Second, you'll distinguish admin and application user identities, understanding who should perform enrollment, registration, and day-to-day operations. Third, you will implement and operate a file system–based wallet using the Node. js SDK: create it, check for identities, and import credentials. Fourth, you will register and enroll a new application user with a CA and import the resulting certificate and key into the wallet. Each skill includes a simple verification step so you can confirm competency, like checking the wallet directory for a new identity file. These objectives prepare you to manage identities responsibly and avoid common pitfalls when building Fabric client applications.

Beyond workflows, this chapter teaches practical security decisions. You will learn the risks of storing private keys on local filesystems, and why production systems often use HSMs or cloud key management. We'll explain how the SDK integrates with external key stores, and what measures you should check—file permissions, access control, and secret management—before trusting a wallet on disk. You will also practice spotting two frequent mistakes: trying to enroll a user before an admin is enrolled, and registering with an incorrect affiliation in multi-organization setups. Each objective includes a short verification step so you can validate your environment. By mastering these practices you reduce the chance of impersonation and make deployments safer for real-world business channels. Objectives: Security and Best Practices means private keys require stronger protection than files; plan for hsms, cloud kms, or strict file permissions in production.. In practical terms, protecting private keys and avoiding common mistakes. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

An identity in Hyperledger Fabric is the cryptographic bundle that proves a requester's identity and authority. Practically, it consists of an X.509 certificate and its matching private key. The certificate contains the public key and identifying attributes issued by the organization’s Certificate Authority; the private key is kept secret and is used to digitally sign transactions. Signing is what binds intent to actions on the ledger and enables authorization checks. A concrete example is an identity labeled Admin@org1. example. com: the certificate lists the subject and any attributes, and the private key proves the admin signed the enrollment or registration calls. A common misconception is that the certificate alone is sufficient; without the private key you cannot sign transactions, so the certificate is not enough to perform authenticated calls. In practice you must protect both parts, and your client code must present them to the Gateway or SDK in a way that keeps the key confidential. To check you understand, inspect the wallet after enrollment and confirm both certificate and private key are stored together. Why does Fabric require this pairing? Because signatures provide non-repudiation and authorization, and the private key is the authority gate.

The Fabric Node. js SDK exposes wallet implementations to manage identities. The two most common are the persistent file system wallet and the ephemeral in-memory wallet. A file system wallet persists credentials to disk so that identities survive application restarts and are available to the Gateway across sessions. This is typically used for long-running client applications and development environments where you want predictable persistence. By contrast, an in-memory wallet keeps identities only in process memory. It is useful for tests, short-lived scripts, or when persistence is not desired for security reasons. A practical example: during development you might use Wallets. newFileSystemWallet to store admin and appUser credentials in a wallet folder. For automated unit tests you might prefer Wallets. newInMemoryWallet so tests start clean each run. A common pitfall is assuming a file system wallet is secure by default; file permissions and storage location matter. For production, plan for external key management; the SDK lets you integrate with hardware or cloud stores. To validate your knowledge, create a wallet, add an identity, restart the application, and confirm the identity persists only with the file system wallet.

Fabric uses a two-step process with the Certificate Authority to add new application users: registration followed by enrollment. Registration is performed by an existing administrator identity and tells the CA about the new user, setting attributes such as enrollment ID, role, and affiliation. The CA returns an enrollment secret after successful registration. Enrollment is the second step where the user or the client acting on behalf of the user sends that secret back to the CA and requests the certificate and key pair. The CA verifies the secret and issues the X.509 certificate and private key material. A concrete scenario is registering appUser under org1. department1; the admin registers with the affiliation and the CA then returns a secret. The client uses that secret in an enroll call to obtain credentials. A typical mistake is trying to enroll without a valid enrollment secret or before the admin is enrolled; both lead to failures. To validate this flow, follow the enrollAdmin and registerUser scripts in the lab: you will see the admin identity imported first, and then the app user after registration and enrollment complete.

Private keys are the single most sensitive element of a Fabric identity: possession of a private key allows an actor to sign transactions as the identity owner, which can enable impersonation and fraudulent ledger actions. For development, filesystem wallets are convenient, but in production you must consider hardened key storage. The chapter recommends Hardware Security Modules (HSMs) or cloud-managed key services like Azure Key Vault as options to remove raw key material from application files. The Fabric SDK exposes interfaces to integrate with such key stores rather than persisting private keys directly in files. Practical mitigations include strict file permissions on wallet directories, limited administrative access to the host, encrypted disks, and auditing of key usage. A common misconception is that encrypting the wallet file is sufficient without access controls; encryption helps, but key lifecycle management, rotation, and revocation policies are equally important. A concrete step is to evaluate whether your deployment requires a managed key service and, if so, plan integration with the Fabric client to delegate signing to that service. Ask yourself: if a private key were lost, how quickly could you revoke it and issue a replacement?

Understanding identity roles is crucial for correct and secure operations. An admin identity is given elevated privileges within an organization’s CA: it can register new users and define their attributes. Admins are typically used only for onboarding identities and should not be used for normal application traffic. Application user identities, such as appUser, are regular user credentials enrolled by the CA and granted the minimal set of permissions required to interact with chaincode. This separation adheres to least privilege: administrative tasks are separated from everyday transactions so an attacker gaining an app user's key cannot perform admin-level actions. A practical example is enrolling an admin to register and enroll an appUser, then configuring your application to use appUser for all Gateway connections. A common mistake is embedding admin credentials into production apps for convenience; this significantly increases risk because those credentials can register or revoke identities. To validate, ensure your app connects using appUser and that wallet contains both admin—used only for registration—and appUser used by the runtime. When working with the CA and wallets you will encounter a few recurrent issues. First, enrollment failures often stem from incorrect CA information in the connection profile—URL, caName, or TLS settings must match the CA configuration. Check the CA entry in your connection-org1. json. Second, attempting to register a user without an enrolled admin or with insufficient admin privileges will fail; confirm admin exists in the wallet and has the right role. Third, incorrect affiliation values during registration are common in multi-organization setups; verify the CA's configured affiliations and use matching strings during registration. Fourth, wallet path confusion: ensure the application and enrollment scripts use the same walletPath so identities are visible to the client. Wallets sit between your client application and two external systems: the Fabric Certificate Authority and the network Gateway. The CA issues credentials during enrollment; the wallet stores those credentials. When your application connects, the Gateway uses the identity retrieved from the wallet to authenticate and sign requests to peers and orderers. Conceptually, the flow is: enroll admin with CA → admin registers a user → user enrolls and credentials are stored in wallet → application retrieves identity from wallet and connects to Gateway. In development, the wallet is often a local filesystem directory; in production, the wallet may be an adapter to an HSM or cloud KMS so private keys never leave the secure store. The architecture highlights the importance of consistent wallet paths, secure storage, and role separation: admin artifacts are only needed for identity lifecycle management, while runtime only needs application identities. These three core ideas summarize the technical essentials you should carry forward. First, an identity is a certificate and private key; both are needed to sign and validate transactions. Second, wallets provide a central mechanism for storing and retrieving identities for client applications; choose file system wallets for persistence and in-memory wallets for ephemeral scenarios. Third, registration and enrollment are separate CA operations: registration returns an enrollment secret and enrollment exchanges that secret for the certificate and key. Keep these distinctions clear as you build and debug your client applications.
